# Abstract  {#abstract}

Financial fraud occurs within complex networks of transactions and financial accounts, yet conventional graph neural networks (GNNs) often assume that connected nodes share similar labels or features. This assumption can fail in heterophilous financial graphs, where fraudulent transactions may be surrounded by legitimate activity, diluting the fraudulent activity. This study will determine whether two heterophily-aware architectural mechanisms, ego neighbor representation separation and explicit second-order neighborhood aggregation, improve fraud classification performance in financial transaction graphs. The mechanisms will be evaluated using data from the Elliptic Bitcoin transaction graph and IEEE-CIS-G from the H2GB benchmark(Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers \- Computational Intelligence Society). Four controlled graph convolutional neural network(GCN) configurations will be compared: baseline GCN, each architecture separately, and both mechanisms combined. Graph structures, node features, labels, and train-validation-test splits will remain fixed, and model settings will be selected using training and validation data before final test evaluation. Each architecture-dataset condition will be trained across five random seeds. Performance will be measured primarily by precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC), with fraud class F1 score and ROC-AUC used as secondary metrics. It is hypothesized that both mechanisms will outperform the baseline and that their combination will produce the greatest improvement because it preserves node-specific information while incorporating structurally distinct information from more distant neighborhoods. If supported, the results would identify specific aggregation mechanisms that improve GNN fraud detection under heterophily and could guide the improvement of graph-based fraud detection systems. 

# Introduction {#introduction}

## The Problem {#the-problem}

Financial crime operates through complex networks of relationships, people, accounts, devices, and transactions. In 2023, an approximate \$3.1 trillion in illicit funds flowed through the global financial system, while fraud scams and bank-fraud schemes produced approximately \$485 billion in global losses([Nasdaq](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1n7Ht6_yx72FGsmtlb564SzNZYkZn7jVQ/view?usp=sharing), 2024, Figure 1). Figure 1 shows a more recent breakdown of U.S. fraud losses and money laundering by category. Traditional fraud detection often evaluates individual transaction features, such as amount and timing, but financial activity is relational. Fraud can be connected through accounts, devices, payment methods, or previous transactions. Transaction data can be represented through graphs, where nodes represent transactions or financial entities and edges represent relationships between them. Graph-based fraud detection can therefore incorporate both node-level information and information from connected entities, furthering the use of relational approaches for fraud classification. ([Weber et al., 2019](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jLPUX6DeO84MBej_0jAQCn6Yb0rNN2Z3/view?usp=sharing))  
![][image1]  
Figure 1: U.S. fraud losses and money laundering in 2025 by category. Data from [Nasdaq Verafin](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1n7Ht6_yx72FGsmtlb564SzNZYkZn7jVQ/view?usp=sharing); figure from [American Banker (2026)](https://www.americanbanker.com/news/ai-and-cartels-push-global-financial-crime-to-4-4-trillion)

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are machine learning models designed to learn from graph data. A GNN updates each node’s representation by combining the node’s own information with information aggregated from its neighbors. This message-passing approach works best when connected nodes tend to share the same labels or characteristics, a property known as homophily ([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing)). Conventional neighborhood aggregation becomes less effective when a fraudulent node is primarily connected to legitimate nodes. In heterophilous graphs, connected nodes may have different labels or features, making neighborhood information less reliable for classification. Financial fraud is a clear example, as fraudulent transactions are often connected to legitimate ones rather than existing only around fraudulent accounts, and fraudsters may deliberately connect to legitimate accounts to disguise their activity. ([Dou et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15y2Rd_ds-IBk_4eecveNNC3CModtkCvU/view?usp=sharing); [Wang et al., 2023](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LZ-GZn0g7dRrmvzxOKaPWdXrttniMcCi/view?usp=sharing))

Previous fraud detection research has identified high heterophily and misleading neighborhoods as challenges for conventional message passing approaches.([Dou et al, 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15y2Rd_ds-IBk_4eecveNNC3CModtkCvU/view?usp=sharing), [Wang et al, 2023\)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LZ-GZn0g7dRrmvzxOKaPWdXrttniMcCi/view?usp=sharing) Under heterophily, aggregating information from legitimate neighbors may dilute or obscure fraudulent features in the target node.([Dou et al, 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15y2Rd_ds-IBk_4eecveNNC3CModtkCvU/view?usp=sharing)) Zhu et al.(2020) identified two specific design changes that improve GNN performance under heterophily: ego-neighbor representation separation and explicit higher-order neighborhood aggregation. However, they evaluated these principles on general benchmark graphs, such as citation and web-page networks, not on financial transaction graphs. As a result, the individual and combined effects of these two mechanisms on fraud classification in financial transaction graphs remain understudied.

 

## Heterophily-Aware Neighborhood Aggregation {#heterophily-aware-neighborhood-aggregation}

Prior fraud detection research indicates that neighborhood aggregation can become unreliable when fraudulent nodes are connected to misleading or legitimate neighbors. ([Dou et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15y2Rd_ds-IBk_4eecveNNC3CModtkCvU/view?usp=sharing), [Wang et al., 2023](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LZ-GZn0g7dRrmvzxOKaPWdXrttniMcCi/view?usp=sharing)) CARE-GNN was developed to address this issue by identifying and selecting more informative neighboring nodes, showing that total aggregation of neighbors can reduce performance. ([Dou et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15y2Rd_ds-IBk_4eecveNNC3CModtkCvU/view?usp=sharing)). More recently, group-aggregated enhanced transformers (GAGA) identified low homophily as a persistent challenge for graph-based fraud detection and showed that modifying how neighboring information is grouped and aggregated can improve classification in highly heterophilous settings ([Wang et al., 2023](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LZ-GZn0g7dRrmvzxOKaPWdXrttniMcCi/view?usp=sharing)). Together, these findings show that the aggregation process is an important target for improving GNN performance on fraud graphs and provide a basis for testing. Table 1 summarizes these fraud-specific studies alongside [Zhu et al. (2020)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing), whose general findings on heterophily provide the basis for the two mechanisms tested in this study.

One example is ego neighbor representation separation. In a conventional Graph Convolutional Network(GCN), a node’s representation is repeatedly updated by averaging information from the node itself with information from its neighbors. Under heterophily, this mixing can dilute the target node’s own features. Table 2 compares the GCN with other common GNN architectures, showing how each aggregates information from neighbors, the main limitation of each, and examples of each. [Zhu et al. (2020)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing) identified ego neighbor separation as an effective design for combating dilution. ([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing)) Instead of immediately averaging the two information sources, the node’s own representation is maintained separately from the aggregated group of neighbors before the representations are combined. Zhu et al. found that architectures preserving this separation performed substantially better than conventional GCN-style aggregation under heterophily. ([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing)) In financial fraud graphs, this mechanism is particularly relevant because a fraudulent node may contain fraudulent features while being surrounded by legitimate neighbors. ([Dou et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.08692); [Wang et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.10407)) Maintaining the ego and neighborhood representations separately may preserve information that would have been diluted.

A second mechanism is explicit higher-order neighborhood aggregation. In a conventional GCN, each layer aggregates information only from a node’s immediate neighbors, while information from more distant nodes is incorporated indirectly through repeated message-passing layers. Zhu et al. instead proposed explicitly aggregating information from neighborhoods at different graph distances. ([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing)) In this framework, first-order (1 hop) neighbors are nodes one edge from the target node, while second-order (2 hops) neighbors are nodes that are 2 edges away. (Figure 2\) Their analysis showed that although immediate neighborhoods may be heterophilous, higher-order neighborhoods can contain different and potentially more informative class structure, making explicit higher-order aggregation beneficial under some heterophilous conditions. This differs from standard modification of GCN depth because first- and second-order neighborhood information remain distinguishable rather than being obtained only through repeated mixing. [(Zhu et al., 2020\)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing) In financial transaction graphs, where fraud can take multiple steps through accounts, explicit second-order aggregation may therefore provide useful structural information that is not available from the immediate neighborhood alone.

Zhu et al. combined ego neighbor separation, higher-order neighborhoods, and intermediate representation combination into H2GCN and demonstrated that these design principles can improve node classification under heterophily([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing)). However, the proposed study will not evaluate H2GCN as a single packaged architecture. Instead, each principle will be implemented independently within a controlled GCN, and higher-order aggregation will be tested in its second-order form, using neighborhoods up to two edges away. Four configurations will be compared: a baseline containing neither, ego-separation only, second-order only, and a combined configuration containing both. Figure 2 shows how each of the four configurations combines information from the target node and its neighborhoods. This design will allow the individual and combined effects of each mechanism to be evaluated, providing a novel controlled comparison of heterophily-aware mechanisms in financial fraud graphs.

## Financial Transaction Graphs and Fraud Classification Performance

The proposed architectural mechanisms will be evaluated on two public financial fraud graphs: the Elliptic Bitcoin transaction graph and IEEE-CIS-G from the H²GB benchmark. Elliptic represents Bitcoin transactions as nodes and payment flows as directed edges, with labeled transactions categorized as licit or illicit ([Weber et al., 2019](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jLPUX6DeO84MBej_0jAQCn6Yb0rNN2Z3/view?usp=sharing)). The dataset contains more than 200,000 transactions, of which only 2% are labeled illicit and 21% licit: the rest are unlabeled ([Weber et al., 2019](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jLPUX6DeO84MBej_0jAQCn6Yb0rNN2Z3/view?usp=sharing)). Because previous studies have used it to classify illicit transactions, it provides a suitable benchmark. 

IEEE-CIS-G provides a structurally different system. It represents the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection dataset as a heterogeneous graph where transaction nodes are indirectly linked through shared metadata such as card information, address, and email. The H²GB benchmark was developed to evaluate graph learning under heterogeneity and heterophily and provides a train, validation, and test split ([Lin et al., 2025](https://drive.google.com/file/d/107KWBoIGqQ6ZG7jxJOucyqV98UymdJXb/view?usp=sharing)). Testing the same independent variables on both Elliptic and IEEE-CIS-G will properly evaluate whether the implementation's results persist across different financial graphs.

Fraud classification performance will be measured using PR-AUC, fraud class F1 score, and ROC-AUC. PR-AUC will serve as the primary measurement because precision-recall analysis directly evaluates performance on the minority positive class and is particularly informative for highly imbalanced classification tasks ([Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IDv7jRJpl3kLfSpqfkER7BwuoH5OTVhD/view?usp=sharing)). The fraud-class F1 score will measure the balance between precision and recall at a selected classification threshold, while ROC-AUC will measure how well the model ranks fraudulent observations above legitimate observations across thresholds. Because ROC-AUC can appear optimistic under severe class imbalance, it will be assessed alongside PR-AUC and F1([Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IDv7jRJpl3kLfSpqfkER7BwuoH5OTVhD/view?usp=sharing)).

Together, the two model systems and three performance metrics will allow the effects of ego neighbor separation and explicit second-order neighborhood aggregation to be evaluated across structurally different graphs. 

## Hypothesis and Implications {#hypothesis-and-implications}

If ego neighbor representation separation and explicit second-order neighborhood aggregation improve the ability of GNNs to learn from heterophilous financial transaction graphs, then either mechanism is expected to return higher PR-AUC, F1 score, and ROC-AUC than the baseline GCN configuration, and the combination of both mechanisms is expected to produce the greatest improvement. This is because it simultaneously preserves node-specific information and incorporates structurally different information from more distant layers. This prediction is supported by prior findings that heterophily reduces the effectiveness of conventional neighborhood aggregation and that separating ego and neighbor representation and explicitly incorporating higher-order neighborhoods can improve results ([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing))  

If supported, these results would demonstrate that the way neighborhood information is aggregated is an important factor in fraud classification rather than the choice of a broader GNN architecture. By isolating the effects of the two independent variables, the study could identify which mechanisms contribute the most to improved fraud classification. These findings could guide the development of future graph-based fraud detection systems that better preserve informative signals when fraudulent activity is present. 

# Research or Engineering Goal {#research-or-engineering-goal}

The goal of this study is to determine how each architecture, ego neighbor representation separation and explicit order neighborhood aggregation, individually and in combination, affect fraud classification performance in the Elliptic and IEEE-CIS-G datasets using a controlled GCN-style architecture.

The three measurable endpoints used to evaluate these effects will be:

- PR-AUC, the primary endpoint for minority class fraud detection performance  
- Fraud-class F1 score, measuring the balance between precision and recall for illicit nodes  
- ROC-AUC, measuring overall ability to distinguish illicit and licit transactions across classification thresholds.

# Methodology {#methodology}

## System Environment & Materials {#system-environment-&-materials}

The study will use the publicly available Elliptic Bitcoin dataset and IEEE-CIS-G from the H²GB benchmark, including their published graph structures, node features, and labels. Both datasets will be split by time to prevent temporal leeakage, so a model is never trained on transactions that occur after the ones it is evaluated on. IEE-CIS-G will use the time-ordered train, validation, and test split published with H2GB ([Lin et al., 2025](https://drive.google.com/file/d/107KWBoIGqQ6ZG7jxJOucyqV98UymdJXb/view?usp=sharing)). Elliptic contains 49 time steps with no edges between different time steps, but it does not include a validation split ([Weber et al., 2019](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jLPUX6DeO84MBej_0jAQCn6Yb0rNN2Z3/view?usp=sharing)). Following Weber et al. (2019), time steps 1-34 will be used for model development and time steps 35- 49 for testing: within model development, time steps 1-29 will be used for training and 30-34 for validation. During each pass, message passing will use only nodes and edges from that split and earlier splits, including unlabeled nodes from those time periods, and only training labels will be used to compute the loss.

Models will be implemented in Python using PyTorch Geometric for graph processing and model training. Scikit-learn will be used to calculate PR-AUC, fraud class F1 score, and ROC-AUC, while NumPy and Pandas will be used for data preparation and processing. SciPy and statmodels will be used for statistical testing. Exact software and package versions will be maintained consistently over the entire study. 

Training will be performed using an A40 NVIDIA GPU with 48GB of VRAM on a cloud server. The same environment will be maintained over each study to reduce variation. The total computational cost of the entire study is estimated to range from \$800 to \$1,400, with the GPU costing \$0.48/Hr to \$2/Hr. The high cost is mainly due to the high demand for high-end GPUs and the inflated price of RAM. No physical equipment or laboratory is needed.

Figure 3 gives an overview of the study: the two datasets and their fixed inputs, the four model configurations, the training procedure, the evaluation metrics, and the computing environment used throughout.

## Experimental Design {#experimental-design}

A controlled 2 x 2 comparison will be conducted on the Elliptic and IEEE-CIS-G financial graphs. Two factors will be manipulated: ego-neighbor representation separation (present or absent) and explicit second-order neighborhood aggregation (present or absent). This produces four GCN-style configurations: A. Baseline GCN, B. Ego-neighbor separation only, C. Second-order aggregation only, and D. Both mechanisms combined.

The published graph structures, node features, labels, and data splits will remain fixed across all runs.   
Edges in both graphs will be treated as undirected for message passing. Unlabeled Elliptic nodes will remain in the graph for message passing but will not contribute to the training loss or evaluation. 

IEEE-CIS-G requires one additional step because it is a bipartite graph: transaction nodes connect only to metadata nodes, and the metadata nodes have no features of their own ([Lin et al., 2025](https://drive.google.com/file/d/107KWBoIGqQ6ZG7jxJOucyqV98UymdJXb/view?usp=sharing)). Because the GCN-Style configurations use a single node type, all nodes will be replaced in one graph, and featureless metadata nodes will receive learnable embeddings, following the G2GB encoding procedure ([Lin et al., 2025](https://drive.google.com/file/d/107KWBoIGqQ6ZG7jxJOucyqV98UymdJXb/view?usp=sharing)). As a result, a transaction’s first-order neighbors in IEEE-CIS-G are metadata nodes, and its second-order neighbors are other transactions that share the same metadata. This structural difference from Elliptic, where transactions connect directly, will be considered when comparing the effect of second-order aggregation between datasets. 

All four configurations will use the same number of layers, hidden dimension, optimizer, maximum number of epochs, and class-weighted loss function, so the presence or absence of each mechanism is the only difference between them. Model settings (learning rate, hidden dimension, and dropout) will be selected using only the training and validation data, and each configuration will receive the same search over these settings. Training will stop when validation PR-AUC fails to improve for a predetermined number of epochs. Final settings will be decided on before test set evaluation to prevent data leakage.

Each architecture-dataset condition will be trained independently five times using different random seeds, which control weight initialization and dropout, producing 40 final runs (4 configs x 2 datasets x 5 seeds). 

### Build Procedure

**1\. Preparing the graphs.** Elliptic will be loaded with PyTorch Geometric’s built-in Elliptic loader, and IEEE-CIS-G will be loaded through the open-source G2GB Python library, which provides the graph in PyTorch Geometric format with its published split. ([Lin et al., 2025](https://drive.google.com/file/d/107KWBoIGqQ6ZG7jxJOucyqV98UymdJXb/view?usp=sharing)). For each dataset, edges will be made undirected by adding a reverse copy of every edge, and node features will be standardized using the mean and standard deviation of the training nodes only, so no information from validation or test nodes enters training. Each node will then be marked as training, validation, or test according to the time-based splits, and IEEE-CIS-G will be merged into a single graph as described above. Finally, the second-order neighbor list of every node will be computed once before training.

**2\. Measure heterophily.** Before training, the homophily of each graph will be measured to confirm that it is heterophilous. For Elliptic, the edge homophily ratio, the fraction of edges between labeled nodes that connect nodes of the same class, will be calculated ([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing)). The same measure will be conducted for IEEE-CIS-G. 

**3\. Build the four configurations.** All four configurations share the same structure. AN input layer, two aggregation layers, and an output layer that classifies each transaction with a fraud probability. Only the aggregation layer differs, as different architectures are applied. ([Zhu et al., 2020](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LjYVCMwxWjfU-DrvMULULESwX6W5V23X/view?usp=sharing))

**4\. Tuning and training.** Models will be trained with the Adam optimizer and class-weighted loss. Each configuration will test the same eight combinations of learning rate. The training will stop after 50 epochs without improvement in validation PR-AUC. The best setting will be frozen before testing.

**5\. Run and final experiments.** The baseline GCN on Elliptic will first be checked against the F1 score of about 0.63 reported by [Weber et al. (2019)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jLPUX6DeO84MBej_0jAQCn6Yb0rNN2Z3/view?usp=sharing) to confirm the system works.  The 40 final runs will then be completed, and each run’s test metrics will be saved to a results table.

## Experimental Assessment {#experimental-assessment}

After each training run, model predictions on the fixed test set will be used to calculate the three dependent variables. The performance will be calculated using scikit-learn.

### PR-AUC {#pr-auc}

Precision and recall will be calculated across classification thresholds, and the area under the resulting precision-recall curve will be measured. PR-AUC will serve as the primary performance metric because both datasets contain substantially fewer fraudulent nodes than legitimate nodes.

### F1 Score {#f1-score}

The F1 score for the illicit class will represent the balance between precision and recall. It will be calculated using a classification threshold selected on the validation set and then applied unchanged to the test set.

### ROC-AUC {#roc-auc}

ROC-AUC will be calculated by comparing each model’s predicted fraud probabilities with the actual fraud labels in the test set. This metric will measure the model’s ability to rank fraudulent nodes above legitimate nodes across classification thresholds. 

Each measurement will be recorded for all five independently seeded runs of every architecture/dataset setup.

## Data Analysis {#data-analysis}

For each architecture/dataset layout, PR-AUC, Fraud-class F1, and ROC-AUC will be summarized as the mean ± standard error of the mean across the five independent training runs. PR-AUC will be the primary measure used, while F1 and ROC-AUC will provide additional performance data.

Each dataset will be analyzed separately to determine how ego neighbor separation and second-order neighborhood aggregation affect model performance, both individually and together. Results with p \< 0.05 will be considered significant. 

Analyzing Elliptic and IEEE-CIS-G separately will allow the study to determine whether the effects of the heterophily-aware mechanisms are consistent across different financial graph structures or perform differently on each dataset.
